record.paper_title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.
record.original_question: Does dividing galaxies into central galaxies, defined as galaxies located at the centers of the most massive or dominant dark matter halos, and satellite galaxies, defined as galaxies in bound subhalos of more massive halos, provide the right framework for studying galaxy evolution across clusters, compact groups, Local-Group-like systems, and other environments?

evidence.quote: Question 3 - Does the central-satellite division provide the right framework to study galaxy evolution?

Galaxies that are located at the center of the most massive, dominant halo are defined as ‘central’ galaxies, and those that are in bound subhalos of more massive halos are defined as ‘satellite’ galaxies.
But how accurately can we correctly identify galaxies as either centrals or satellites?
Therefore it is possible that the central/satellite framework may be failing to capture the interesting effects of environment on the evolution of many galaxies.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In the standard cosmological picture, galaxies form within dark matter halos. Define a central galaxy to be a galaxy located at the center of the most massive (dominant) dark matter halo of a given system, and a satellite galaxy to be a galaxy residing in a gravitationally bound subhalo of a more massive host halo. Consider the full range of environments in which galaxies are found, including rich clusters, compact groups, Local-Group-like systems, loose groups, filaments, and isolated field environments.

Determine whether the binary classification of galaxies into centrals and satellites, as defined above, constitutes an adequate framework for describing and studying galaxy evolution across all such environments. Specifically, address the following:

(a) To what extent can galaxies be unambiguously and accurately identified as either central or satellite, given observational uncertainties in halo membership and the dynamical complexity of group/cluster environments?

(b) Are there environmental processes affecting galaxy evolution (e.g., pre-processing in infalling groups, tidal interactions in compact groups, backsplash galaxies, or dynamics in Local-Group-like pairs) whose effects are not captured by the central/satellite dichotomy?

(c) Provide either a justification that the central/satellite division is sufficient as the organizing framework for galaxy evolution studies, or identify a more refined classification scheme that better captures the dependence of galaxy evolution on environment.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a conceptual open problem in galaxy formation rather than a settled mathematical theorem. Subsequent literature on satellite quenching, pre-processing, splashback/backsplash galaxies, and orphan/fly-by galaxies indicates that the simple central/satellite dichotomy captures much, but not all, environmental influence on galaxy evolution; the framework remains widely used but is acknowledged to be incomplete. No definitive resolution exists.

status_evidence.title: Wetzel et al., Pre-processing of galaxies before infall
status_evidence.snippet: Substantial fraction of satellite galaxies were processed in smaller groups before infall onto the main host, complicating a strict central/satellite dichotomy.
status_evidence.claim: Pre-processing demonstrates limitations of the binary central/satellite framework.

status_evidence.title: Behroozi et al., UniverseMachine
status_evidence.snippet: Modern empirical models still organize galaxy evolution around halo/subhalo (central/satellite) assignments while acknowledging additional environmental dependence.
status_evidence.claim: The central/satellite framework remains the standard but is supplemented by additional environmental variables.
